_note: On-brand comment lines to paste on OTHER people's maritime/PMS/yacht posts — awareness through genuine engagement. Voice: observational, restraint, ex-ETO lived authority. NEVER salesy, never names CelesteOS, never cliché ('Great post!'), no emoji, no banned words. The comment earns the profile click; it never pitches. Edit freely — the agent reads this file.

categories.use_when: Someone posts about engineers rotating off, losing experienced crew, or the handover process
lines: The part that never makes the handover doc is the why — why that valve, why that supplier, why that workaround that's kept a generator running for years. That leaves with the person, not the paperwork.
Every rotation I did as an ETO, the first week was just rebuilding what the last team already knew. The boat had the answers; they just weren't findable.
The handover is the lowest-priority task on the busiest day of a rotation. That's not a discipline problem — it's a structural one.

categories.use_when: Posts about planned maintenance systems, record-keeping, or documentation standards
lines: The record almost always exists. Finding it — and trusting it was written at the time, not reconstructed after — is the actual work.
A maintenance system shows the tasks. The reasoning, the half-resolved threads, the numbers — that usually lives somewhere the system can't see.
Most of the operational truth on a vessel isn't in the PMS. It's in an inbox, a notebook, and one engineer's memory.

categories.use_when: Posts about data buried in email, can't find old reports, information scattered across systems
lines: Finding the right record was never the hard part. Knowing it existed, and where, was.
The inbox tends to hold more of the real operational history than the system does — it's just the one place you can't properly search.
One email thread can carry three quotes, but the subject line names one. The other two aren't lost — they're just unfindable.

categories.use_when: Posts about going paperless, digital transformation, moving off spreadsheets/Word
lines: Paperless only helps if you can find the page. A PDF you can't search is a filing cabinet with extra steps.
Digitising the document isn't the win. Making the thing inside it reachable from anywhere on the vessel is.
Going digital tends to move the mess, not remove it — unless the records actually connect to each other.

categories.use_when: Posts about software adoption, crew not using tools, change management onboard
lines: A system fails the day the second engineer stops opening it. The most capable software loses to the one people actually use.
Adoption isn't a training problem. If a tool costs more effort than the notebook it replaces, the notebook wins — every time.
The quiet test of any onboard system: does it survive a crew change without anyone being told to keep it going.

categories.use_when: Posts about surveys, audits, class, insurance claims, proving what was done
lines: A surveyor doesn't want the story. They want the record — written at the time, by the person who did the work.
The strongest defence in an audit isn't a tidy report. It's a trail that was never reconstructed after the fact.
When the insurer asks what was done on a job from eight months ago, the answer is only as good as where that proof actually lives.

categories.use_when: Posts hyping or doubting AI/tech in shipping; respond to the doubt honestly, never hype
lines: Fair to be sceptical of 'AI' on a boat. The useful question isn't whether it's clever — it's whether it finds what you meant when you're tired and the alarm's going.
Most maritime tech fails the same test: it's impressive in a demo and invisible at 3am when something's actually broken.
The bar isn't intelligence. It's whether the thing reduces the effort of the worst job on the worst day.

categories.use_when: Personal/reflective posts where a grounded ex-ETO perspective fits naturally
lines: Spent years as an ETO opening a different handover format every rotation. The tools changed; the problem didn't.
I've stood in front of an owner pointing at the wrong file, and diagnosed the same fault twice on the same vessel. Neither was a knowledge problem — both were a findability one.
The people who run these boats aren't short on information. They're short on a way to reach the right piece of it at the right moment.
